title: Minimum wage and the jobs argument

turns.speaker: Camila
turns.text: It goes up eight per cent in April and the usual letters have started. Job losses, small businesses, the whole script.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: The script's been running for thirty years and the job losses haven't really shown up, which is the awkward part.

turns.speaker: Rowan
turns.text: That's fair up to a point. The evidence is that moderate rises don't cost jobs. Nobody has evidence about a rise that goes far past the local median.

turns.speaker: Camila
turns.text: So the finding is bounded rather than unlimited.

turns.speaker: Rowan
turns.text: Exactly, and both sides quote it as if it were unlimited in their direction.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Why doesn't it cost jobs, though? The textbook is fairly clear.

turns.speaker: Rowan
turns.text: Because the textbook assumes a worker can move to a competing employer easily, and in a small town with two large employers that simply isn't true.

turns.speaker: Rowan
turns.text: Where the employer has that power, wages sit below what the work produces, so raising them doesn't automatically cut hiring.

turns.speaker: Camila
turns.text: And the adjustment tends to come as prices rather than redundancies.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Which hits the same people who got the rise.

turns.speaker: Camila
turns.text: Some of it. The effect measured is small, though, and they still come out ahead.

turns.speaker: Rowan
turns.text: The part I'd watch is hours. Employers cut shifts before they cut staff, and that never appears in an employment figure.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: So the headline says nothing changed while people are earning less.

points: An eight per cent minimum wage rise prompted the usual warnings about job losses.
Josh notes predicted job losses have largely failed to appear over thirty years.
Rowan qualifies this: evidence supports moderate rises, but not increases far above the local median, and both sides overstate the finding.
The textbook prediction fails because workers often cannot move employers easily, so wages sit below the value produced.
Adjustment tends to come through prices rather than redundancies, though the measured effect is small and workers still gain.
Rowan warns hours are cut before staff, which does not show in employment statistics.
